Some have said that the credit for introducing philosophical principles into Muʿtazilite thought belongs to Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf.
Others have said that al-ʿAllāf was the true founder of kalām among the Muslims, or that he was “the first Islamic theologian to be influenced by philosophy.”
This kind of precise dating may be too rigid.

Intellectual movements, like the many other phenomena that arise in society, cannot normally be assigned to one exact dividing point in time or said to have appeared for the first time in one single individual.
Even so, these claims by both older historians and modern scholars point to the same basic fact.
The relationship between kalām and philosophy appeared very early in history, and the Muʿtazilites played the creative mediating role in bringing that relationship into being.
It is also striking that later theologians developed the relationship between kalām and philosophy even at the level of how they organized and classified their works.
Among them were the author of al-Mawāqif, the author of al-Maqāṣid, and the author of Ṭawāliʿ al-Anwār.
They began to use Aristotle’s arrangement of philosophical subjects as a model for organizing their own theological discussions.
This development was only formal, but it was still historically significant.
These later theologians were working at a time when attacks on philosophy had become more intense and when people who studied philosophy were being persecuted.
Yet all those attacks still failed to break the connection between kalām and philosophy, or between Arab-Islamic thought more generally and philosophy.
In fact, the opposite seems to have happened.
The relationship continued to reassert itself in new forms, adapted to the particular intellectual movements and historical conditions of each period.

A brief digression is useful here. The point is not really about philosophy for its own sake. It is about development in general, and about the intellectual freedom that development requires. It is also about the need for seeds of liberation to survive for as long as development still needs them, however powerful or cunning the forces of repression may be. The very existence of philosophy, in any form at all, was itself an encouraging sign. It showed that those seeds were still alive and still capable of challenging the rule of backward theological thought.

It is true that by the time of the later theologians, in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, much philosophical thought had begun to harden into conventional forms. It often lost its vitality and its ability to absorb the realities of its own age. Yet the attacks and persecution, which were still growing more intense at the time, were aimed at the rational content of philosophy—the philosophy that was then carrying the torch of a challenge to a theological ideology already in crisis.

To sum up what we have said so far: from its beginnings with the Muʿtazila, kalām gradually found its way toward philosophy, both in subject matter and in method. Even before kalām became an organized discipline, its questions and debates gave Arab-Islamic thought its first route toward philosophical thinking. They provided the necessary preparation for this kind of thought to develop, under its particular historical conditions, into a higher stage than kalām itself: the stage of philosophy.
This brings us to our second question:
What were the limits of the relationship between kalām and philosophy?
We have said that each was a relatively independent stage in the development of Arab-Islamic thought. That fact already gives us a first indication of the boundary between them.

A more precise answer comes from looking at the role each one played. Kalām used philosophical thinking as a way of examining questions that had arisen directly within Arab society after Islam, but it dealt with them in the form of religious debate about doctrine.

Philosophy, by contrast, emerged in Arab-Islamic society after kalām had reached maturity. It dealt with existence, nature, society, and thought as concepts in their own right. In those concepts, the material world was reflected indirectly, as a particular society with its own historical conditions, characteristics, and forms of social relations.
Philosophy therefore differed from kalām in two basic ways.
First, it began from concepts rather than from questions arising directly within society.

Second, it did not take the doctrines of Islam as the starting point of its inquiry. It did try to hide the contradictions between the conclusions reached through philosophical investigation and the doctrines of Islamic faith. These attempts later came to be described as a “reconciliation” between philosophy and religion, though that description is inaccurate.
5 — The Contradiction Between Kalām and Philosophy

The dialectic of the relationship between kalām and philosophy inevitably contained serious contradictions. These became clear once each began to need a degree of independence from the other, around the middle of the third century AH, or after the middle of the ninth century CE.

Perhaps the most important source of these contradictions was this: when kalām reached maturity in its Muʿtazilite stage, it had already come close to philosophical thinking by giving reason a broad role in thought and in the search for knowledge, even in questions beyond nature.

According to the general laws of development, kalām should therefore have given way to philosophy in the further development of Arab-Islamic thought. Kalām had fulfilled the need that had brought it into existence and had exhausted its historical tasks. The time had come for it to develop into philosophy proper.
But events took a different course.
A conservative reaction against Muʿtazilite thought arose during the reign of the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil. Then came the Ashʿarite school of kalām, which expressed this reaction in a new form.

The result was not what might otherwise have been expected. Muʿtazilite kalām was replaced, on one side, by Ashʿarite kalām and, on the other, by a philosophical movement that had separated itself from kalām as a whole.
The transformation was therefore contradictory from the very beginning. In practice, it produced two opposing poles: philosophy and Ashʿarite kalām.

This explains the historical pattern we have already seen: open hostility and sometimes violent conflict between post-Muʿtazilite kalām and the different philosophical movements, from the Brethren of Purity to the philosophy of Ibn Rushd.
The antagonism between them had an ideological basis from the outset.

As we have seen, Ashʿarite kalām marked a return toward Sunni traditionalism. Its purpose was to tear down the rational structure that Muʿtazilite thought had built. The Ashʿarites tried to present themselves as “rational,” but, as we noted earlier, this rationalism remained largely formal.
From that point onward, it became increasingly clear that the conflict between kalām and philosophy was, above all, an ideological conflict.
Kalām came to express the “official” ideology. Philosophy, together with Sufism, increasingly expressed the outlook of different social groups opposed to the central ruling authority.

The evidence is the persecution that philosophy suffered in different forms over many centuries. It often began as intellectual persecution in the writings of theologians and then became material and physical persecution at the hands of the ruling authorities.

Why, for example, were the copyists of Baghdad required in 277 AH to swear that they would not copy books on philosophy, to the point that some copyists abandoned their profession altogether? In our own age, forcing copyists to abandon their trade would be equivalent to shutting down the printing presses.
And why did hostility to philosophy eventually spread to almost everything that could be included under the broad heading of science?

The Kitāb al-Aghānī tells us that Abū Zayd al-Balkhī was accused of unbelief simply because he was “engaged in gathering the ancient and modern sciences, and in his writings followed the method of the philosophers.”
Aristotle’s metaphysics in particular became a target of anger among the Sunnis:

Aristotle’s metaphysics was, first and foremost, an object of anger among the Sunnis. They regarded both its premises and its conclusions as completely opposed to the requirements of Islamic belief. Their anger went further and came to include the mathematical sciences as well, because these prepared the way for philosophical study. Geometry, for example, became a cause for suspicion among the Sunnis. Geometrical figures made them uneasy and could cause their owner to be accused of heresy. (...) Abū al-Ḥasan ibn Fāris, in his book al-Ṣāḥibī fī Fiqh al-Lugha wa-Sunan al-ʿArab fī Kalāmihā, spoke of the danger that geometry posed to religion and of its limited usefulness. He concluded that engaging in mathematics led a person to abandon religion.

From this picture, we can also see why it was no accident that theological reaction in medieval Europe made use of al-Ghazālī’s Ashʿarite and anti-philosophical arguments as a weapon against forms of philosophy that opposed theological philosophy.

R. Martin, a contemporary of Thomas Aquinas, did this, for example, in his book The Defence of Faith. He wrote it at the request of Raymond Puniaforte, head of the Dominican order, and incorporated many of al-Ghazālī’s ideas into it.

This was not a coincidence. It was one sign of the way the ideological struggle moved, by the end of the fourteenth century, from its old arena in the East to a new arena in Europe. Arab-Islamic society had begun to decline economically, socially, politically, and culturally, while the seeds of the European Renaissance were beginning to grow in an atmosphere of technical progress whose first signs appeared near the end of the Middle Ages.

This shift also helps explain Ibn Khaldūn’s statement, at the end of the fourteenth century, that “kalām is no longer necessary for the student in this age, since the unbelievers and innovators have disappeared.”

By “unbelievers and innovators,” Ibn Khaldūn of course meant the philosophers and all those whose ideas and tendencies led them to give philosophical explanations of the truths of the universe outside the unseen world. In other words, he meant the whole intellectual and ideological camp that Ashʿarite kalām opposed and fought against.
But had these people really disappeared by Ibn Khaldūn’s time, leaving only the Ashʿarite theologians in the field?

It seems to us that this was not really a matter of one side disappearing and the other remaining alone. Rather, the very subject of the ideological struggle in the East was beginning to lose its foundation, because the society that had formed the basic ground of that struggle was itself collapsing.

At the same time, a new society was emerging in the West—in Europe. It was preparing to become the new subject of the struggle and the more active arena of a class conflict that would be intense and would eventually give birth to a new world, bringing humanity new kinds of social relations.
At the end of this chapter, we can give a short and concentrated conclusion that also serves as a complete summary of the second part of our study:

During its first stage, from the end of the first century AH to the end of the first third of the third century AH, kalām consisted of philosophical practices and ideological reflections that took religious doctrine as the form through which they appeared and developed. This continued until kalām had completed its preparatory role and the conditions were ready for the emergence of an Arab philosophy independent of it.

A scientific study of history shows us that gradual, quantitative changes in the development of society can take different forms when they produce a qualitative change. They may produce a political, social, or intellectual and theoretical change, for example, or they may take the form of revolutionary violence.

Seen in this light, we can follow the process of accumulation in Arab-Islamic society during the seventh and eighth centuries. Among the different qualitative changes that grew out of this process, kalām became the most advanced intellectual form.
We saw that this accumulation began after the death of the Prophet. First came the struggle over the caliphate, followed by conflict over the material advantages attached to that powerful office.

We also saw that the establishment of the Umayyad state was the first major political transformation produced by this accumulation of events. It was supported by economic and social changes, and it also produced a new intellectual form.

The economic side of this transformation lay in the fact that Umayyad political power became an active participant in the system of feudal relations of production. It protected that system and helped develop it and renew its productive forces, especially in Syria.

This economic structure also shaped the social side of the transformation. Once the Umayyad state became involved in economic activity within feudal relations of production, the character of social relations and of the wider social system was necessarily affected.
The intellectual side first appeared through three competing theories: the Umayyad theory, the ʿAlid or Shiʿi theory, and the Khārijite theory.

But the relationship between quantitative accumulation and qualitative change could not stop there. Permanent change is the basic revolutionary feature of the dialectic between quantity and quality. Every new qualitative form is itself subjected to further gradual changes, which eventually lead to new qualitative transformations, and so the process continues.

In the first volume of this study, we showed how new contradictions began to develop within feudal relations of production during the Umayyad period. These contradictions accumulated and then produced new qualitative forms: political, social, intellectual, and theoretical. They were also accompanied by violent forms of struggle, including armed uprisings.
The first new intellectual form was the question of divine decree and predestination.

The rejection of predestination expressed, at the ideological level, the anger of working and educated groups. It was the first voice in Arab thought to rise against the official doctrine built on the idea of predestination.
Cultural interaction then introduced new ways of thinking about these problems. Thinkers began to develop principles for dealing with them in more advanced ways.
The Muʿtazila were the pioneers of this development. They relied above all on reason, both in gaining knowledge and in dealing with questions of society and religious belief.

At first, however, their investigations were still a collection of discussions without a systematic structure. Arab-Islamic thought had not yet reached the stage at which each kind of intellectual and theoretical inquiry could be given its own distinct scholarly identity.

Once it reached that stage, fields of knowledge were classified. Islamic jurisprudence became an independent discipline, and kalām became another independent discipline. The first dealt with the legal rulings of Islamic law, while the second dealt with the foundations of Islamic belief.
Most historical sources agree that this classification took shape during the reign of the Abbasid caliph al-Maʾmūn. Al-Shahrastānī, for example, says this in al-Milal wa-l-Niḥal, vol. 1, p. 32.

The name kalām, in our view, probably became established because the word had already been used in earlier theological debates, before kalām became a formal discipline. People would say, for example, that a certain person “had something to say”—kalām—about predestination, or that someone else did not like to “speak”—kalām—about the attributes of God. We quoted a historical text earlier as an example of this usage.

The writing of works on kalām began before it had become a formal discipline with its own concepts and categories. It began with the wider movement to record knowledge in writing during the first century AH, or the seventh century CE.
Some sources tell us this, but none of the works from that period dealing with questions of kalām have survived, even though works on other subjects have reached us.
It seems that the writings of the early theologians, especially the Muʿtazila, were deliberately suppressed because they challenged the official thought and ideology of the state.

After the first century, writing on kalām became much more active, especially from the reign of al-Maʾmūn onward. Works of kalām became the main intellectual arena in which theoretical and ideological struggles appeared.
They remained so until philosophy emerged and took over the leading role in theoretical and ideological thought.
The surviving definitions of kalām do not include any definition written by the Muʿtazila themselves.
What we have is a definition from al-Fārābī, followed by definitions from Ashʿarite theologians.
For this reason, these definitions do not fully reflect the real nature of kalām or its basic features. We gave examples of them from their original sources earlier in the chapter.

Even al-Fārābī’s definition does not fully reflect how far the Muʿtazila relied on reason. We showed this by comparing his definition with the well-known role that reason played in Muʿtazilite thought. Al-Fārābī’s text comes from his Enumeration of the Sciences, pp. 107–108.
If we relied only on Ashʿarite definitions, we would get a distorted picture of kalām.
For that reason, we approached the problem through the Muʿtazilite movement itself and through the way the Muʿtazila thought.
From this discussion, we reached two conclusions.

First, kalām is the name given to a set of questions expressed in religious terms. Debate over these questions was first driven by different forms of social and political conflict beginning in the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. Other questions were then added as the multiethnic Arab-Islamic society continued to develop.
Intellectual development later moved these debates into increasingly abstract forms, to the point that their social dimensions could almost disappear from view.
Even so, a scientific approach can still see that the basic starting points behind the differing opinions and positions on these questions lay in concrete social realities.
Second, kalām passed through two main stages in its history: the stage of Muʿtazilite kalām and the stage of Ashʿarite kalām.
This does not mean we should forget the other theologians among the Shiʿa, Khārijites, Murjiʾa, Jabriyya, and Sufis.
Our division of the history of kalām into these two stages is based on our conclusion that two main tendencies ran through its entire history.
The first was the rationalist tendency. It treated reason as the main basis for gaining knowledge about religious belief, nature, and society. This was the tendency of the Muʿtazila.

The second was the opposing tendency, which relied on knowledge of the unseen rather than on reason. This was the tendency of those known as the People of the Sunna. The Ashʿarites became its main representatives and used it to fight the first tendency throughout the later centuries.
We have argued that the Ashʿarite stage was essentially a reaction against the Muʿtazilite stage.
We also concluded that this reaction was fundamentally ideological, while religion provided its historical form.
From its beginnings, Ashʿarite kalām became the doctrine of the caliphal state and remained so until that state collapsed. This supports our view of its ideological character.

The most important feature of the Muʿtazilite rationalist method was its attempt to “rationalize” the whole metaphysics of Islam. Its aim was to give reason the freedom to think without being bound in advance by predestination.
